name: Prompt Caching
question: Am I paying again for the same prompt prefix?
summary: Providers can store the processed form of a long, unchanging prompt prefix, such as the system prompt, tool definitions and reference documents, and reuse it on the next call. Cached input is billed at a fraction of the normal price and is processed faster. A separate response cache can skip the model entirely for repeated questions.
useCases: Agents that resend the same system prompt and tools on every step
Chat over a fixed document, codebase or knowledge pack
Many users sharing one long instruction set

items.detail: the longest stable prefix: system prompt, tools, documents, earlier turns
cached input tokens ÷ total input tokens
cached reads cost a fraction of normal input
providers require a minimum prefix, often around 1,024 tokens
minutes by default, refreshed on each hit
reuse whole answers for near-duplicate questions

steps: Order the prompt: static content first, variable content (user message, date) last
Mark the cache breakpoint where your provider requires it, or rely on automatic caching
Keep timestamps, request IDs and shuffled examples out of the prefix
Watch hit rate. A sudden drop usually means something changed in the prefix
pitfalls: One changed character early in the prompt invalidates everything after it
Cache writes can cost more than normal input on some providers
Semantic caches can serve a stale or wrong answer to a subtly different question
caption: Units = base input price per token. Uses Anthropic’s published multipliers: cache write 1.25×, cache read 0.1×.

code.text: model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=1024,       # use your current model
r2 = ask("List the key risks.")                  # within 5 minutes
print(f"hit rate {cached / total:.0%}")          # alert if this drops

steps.title: Order the prompt
steps.text: Caching works on the prefix, in the order tools, system, messages. Put everything that never changes first and the question last.

steps.title: Mark the breakpoint
steps.text: cache_control marks the end of the stable prefix. Everything up to it, 12,000 tokens here, is cached for 5 minutes by default.

steps.title: The first call writes the cache
steps.text: Call 1 processes the prefix and stores it. The write costs 1.25× the normal input price, slightly more than no caching.

steps.title: The next call reads it
steps.text: Call 2 arrives within 5 minutes with an identical prefix, so the 12,000 tokens bill at 0.1×. Only the question is new.

steps.title: One changed byte breaks it
steps.text: The date is safe in the user message. Move it into the system text above the breakpoint and every call misses and rewrites.

steps.title: Monitor the hit rate
steps.text: Read the usage fields on every response. Over a 20-call session this prefix hits 19 times and input cost falls by 83%.

pros: Large savings on long, repeated prefixes: cached reads bill at a fraction of input price
Faster time to first token on long prompts
Little code: reorder the prompt and mark a breakpoint
Stacks with batch processing and routing
cons: Any change before the breakpoint invalidates the cache
Cache writes can cost more than normal input
Entries expire after minutes without traffic
Minimum prefix sizes rule out short prompts
avoidWhen: Prompts are short or different on every call
Calls are hours apart, so the cache always expires

playgroundGuide.scenario: An equity research agent answers an analyst's questions about one annual report. Every call sends the same tools, instructions and report, then a short question. You control how big that stable prefix is, how many calls the session makes and how far apart they are, and whether something breaks the cache.
controls: Drag the sliders to set the prefix size and the number of calls.
Choose the time between calls and the cache lifetime.
Turn caching on, and try putting a timestamp at the top of the system prompt.

outputs.name: Input cost vs no caching
outputs.meaning: Session input cost with your settings as a share of the uncached cost. Above 100% means caching costs extra.

outputs.name: Cache hit rate
outputs.meaning: Tokens read from the cache ÷ all input tokens sent.

outputs.name: Cache writes · reads
outputs.meaning: How many calls wrote the prefix (billed at 1.25× or 2×) and how many read it (0.1×).

outputs.name: Saving on input
outputs.meaning: The percentage cut in input cost. Negative means you pay more than without caching.

presets.name: No caching
presets.expect: 20 calls pay full price for a 12,000-token prefix: $0.732 per session, hit rate 0%.

presets.name: Caching on
presets.expect: 1 write and 19 reads: $0.125 per session, hit rate 93%, a saving of 83%.

presets.name: Timestamp at the top
presets.expect: Every call writes and none reads: $0.912 per session, 25% more than no caching.

presets.name: Calls 20 minutes apart
presets.expect: The 5-minute cache expires between calls, so all 20 calls write: again 25% more than no caching.

missions.text: Push the input saving to 85% or more.
missions.hint: With caching on, each extra call costs only a tenth of the prefix. Raise the number of calls to about 35 or more.

missions.text: With calls 20 minutes apart, get the saving above 75%.
missions.hint: Switch to the 1-hour cache lifetime. The write costs 2×, but every later call reads.

missions.text: Turn caching on but find a prefix size where nothing gets cached.
missions.hint: Providers require a minimum prefix. Drag the prefix below 1,024 tokens.

tools.best: Explicit cache breakpoints with 5-minute or 1-hour lifetimes and usage fields that report writes and reads.
tools.ex: Cache a 10,000-token annual report once, then answer 20 analyst questions at the cached rate.
pros: Precise control over what is cached
Usage fields make hit rates easy to monitor
cons: Writes cost more than normal input

tools.best: Automatic caching of long prompt prefixes with no code changes.
tools.ex: A support bot with a 3,000-token system prompt sees cached_tokens rise in usage as soon as prompts are reordered.
cons: Less control over what is cached and for how long

tools.best: Implicit caching on recent models plus explicit caches with a lifetime you set.

pros: Explicit caches suit very large, long-lived context
cons: Explicit caches have storage costs over time

tools.best: A semantic response cache that returns stored answers for similar questions without calling the model.

pros: Skips the model call entirely on a hit
Pluggable embedding and storage back ends
cons: Similar is not identical: risk of wrong answers
Less active than it once was

pros: Production-grade store many teams already run
Thresholds and expiry under your control
cons: Tuning the similarity threshold takes care

practice.scenario: A research agent for equity analysts sends a 12,000-token prompt on each of 20 steps: instructions, tool definitions and a company's annual report. With the report marked for caching, the first step writes it to the cache and the next 19 read it at the cached rate.

Cache repository context and tool definitions across agent steps

practice.analogy: A chef's mise en place. The chopping is done once before service; each order only needs the final cooking.

library.name: Anthropic SDK (prompt caching)
library.what: Mark the end of the stable prefix with cache_control; the usage object reports cache writes and reads so you can check hit rates.

samples.code:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

report = open("annual_report.txt").read()          # large and unchanging

def ask(question: str):
    return client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5",                  # use your current model
        max_tokens=1024,
        system=[
            {"type": "text", "text": "You are an equity research assistant."},
            {"type": "text", "text": report,
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},   # cache everything up to here
        ],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],   # variable part last
    )

r1 = ask("Summarize segment revenue.")
r2 = ask("List the key risks management mentions.")
print(r1.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens, r2.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)

numericDrill.question: Base input: $3 per million tokens. Cache write 1.25×, read 0.1×. A 20,000-token prefix is used on 10 calls within the cache window. What does the prefix cost with caching, in $?
numericDrill.answer: Without caching: 200,000 tokens × $3/M = $0.60. With caching: one write (20,000 × $3.75/M = $0.075) plus 9 reads (180,000 × $0.30/M = $0.054) = $0.129, about 78% less.

interview.question: What breaks prompt caching?
interview.answer: Any change before the cache breakpoint: timestamps, request IDs, reordered tools or examples, or per-user text in the system prompt. Keep the static prefix byte-identical and put variable content last.

interview.question: How is prompt caching different from semantic caching?
interview.answer: Prompt caching reuses the processed prefix, and the model still generates a fresh answer. Semantic caching returns a stored answer for a similar question without calling the model: cheaper, but it risks stale or wrong answers.

mistakes.mistake: Putting the date or user name at the top of the system prompt
mistakes.fix: Move variable content to the end
Monitor cache read and write tokens per request

quiz.question: A legal assistant sends a 30,000-token contract with each of 25 questions over 10 minutes, but the cache hit rate is 0%. The system prompt begins “Session started at 14:32:07”. What is the cause?
options: The contract is too long to cache
Caching only works with batch jobs
The timestamp at the top changes the prefix on every call
The questions are too short
quiz.explanation: Any change before the breakpoint invalidates the cache. Move the timestamp after the stable content.

quiz.question: Base input is $3 per million tokens, cache writes cost 1.25× and reads 0.1×. A 16,000-token prefix is used on 8 calls within the cache lifetime. What does the prefix cost with caching?
quiz.explanation: One write: 16,000 × $3.75/M = $0.06. Seven reads: 112,000 × $0.30/M = $0.0336. Total $0.0936, against $0.384 uncached.

quiz.question: A 5,000-token catalogue prompt is reused on 40 calls within the cache lifetime. Writes cost 1.25× and reads 0.1× the base input price. What is the saving on the prefix?
Which changes will cause prompt-cache misses on a claims assistant? Select all that apply.
options: Putting each policyholder’s name at the start of the system prompt
Reordering the tool definitions between calls
Changing the question at the end of the prompt
Shuffling the few-shot examples on each call
quiz.explanation: Anything that changes the prefix breaks the cache. The final question sits after the breakpoint, so it is safe.

quiz.question: A support bot’s calls arrive about 30 minutes apart, and the provider’s default cache lifetime is 5 minutes. What happens?
options: Every call reads at 0.1×
Every call writes the cache again, so caching adds cost
The provider keeps the cache for a day
The request fails
quiz.explanation: The entry expires between calls, so each call pays the write premium and nothing is read. A longer lifetime, where offered, fixes it.

quiz.question: A 12,000-token prefix uses a 1-hour cache (writes 2×, reads 0.1×). Calls arrive every 20 minutes for 3 hours: 10 calls. What is the saving on the prefix?
quiz.explanation: One write: 12,000 × 2 = 24,000 units. Nine reads: 9 × 1,200 = 10,800. Total 34,800 against 120,000: a 71.0% saving.

quiz.question: A semantic cache answers “What is the FD rate for 2 years?” with the stored answer for “What is the FD rate for 1 year?”. What went wrong?
options: The prompt cache expired
The batch discount was applied twice
The router picked the wrong model
A near-duplicate match served a stored answer to a different question
quiz.explanation: Semantic caches reuse whole answers for similar questions, so a small but important difference can return a wrong answer.

quiz.question: You use Claude and want explicit control over what is cached, with an option for a 1-hour lifetime. What do you use?
options: GPTCache
Anthropic prompt caching with cache_control
Celery beat
LLMLingua
quiz.explanation: Anthropic’s prompt caching uses cache_control breakpoints and offers 5-minute and 1-hour lifetimes.

quiz.question: What belongs in the cached prefix of an agent’s prompt? Select all that apply.
options: Tool definitions
System instructions
A long reference document
The current user’s message
quiz.explanation: Stable content goes in the prefix. The user’s message changes every call, so it goes after the breakpoint.

quiz.question: A patient-FAQ bot on OpenAI has a 3,000-token system prompt. What do you need to do to benefit from prompt caching?
options: Add cache_control to every message
Send requests through the batch API
Nothing special: caching is automatic for long prompts, so keep the prefix stable
Nothing: OpenAI does not cache prompts
quiz.explanation: OpenAI caches long prompt prefixes automatically. Your job is to keep the start of the prompt identical.

quiz.question: A response’s usage shows 9,000 tokens read from cache, 1,000 uncached input tokens and no cache writes. What is the cache hit rate?
quiz.explanation: Hit rate = cached tokens ÷ all input tokens = 9,000 ÷ 10,000 = 90%.

quiz.question: Which workloads benefit most from prompt caching? Select all that apply.
options: A coding agent resending 40,000 tokens of repository context over 30 steps
Many users sharing one long instruction set
One-off prompts that are different every time
Chat over a fixed product manual
quiz.explanation: Caching pays when a long prefix repeats. Prompts that never repeat get nothing from it.

quiz.question: Prompt caching is turned on for a rebooking agent. Which costs does it NOT reduce? Select all that apply.
options: Output tokens
The new tokens in each user message
Input cost of the repeated prefix
The number of requests
quiz.explanation: Caching discounts only the repeated input prefix. Output, fresh input and request count are unchanged.

quiz.question: After adding a summary step that rewrites the history on every turn, a tutor bot’s cache hit rate fell from 85% to 20%. Why?
options: Summaries increase output tokens
The cache has a daily quota
Rewriting history changes the prefix, so later content no longer matches
The model version changed
quiz.explanation: Caching needs an identical prefix. Prune less often, below the stable system prompt and tools.

quiz.question: Twelve lawyers will query the same 300-page case bundle all afternoon on Gemini. Which approach fits?
options: An explicit context cache with a lifetime that covers the afternoon
A semantic cache keyed by lawyer name
One batch job per question
Prompt compression alone
quiz.explanation: Explicit context caching suits very large context reused many times over a known period.

quiz.question: A merchant-support prompt has an 800-token stable prefix, and the model’s minimum cacheable prefix is 1,024 tokens. What saving does caching give?
options: 0%: the prefix is below the minimum
About 50%
About 75%
About 90%
quiz.explanation: Prefixes below the minimum are not cached at all, so there is nothing to save.

quiz.question: On the Claude API, where do you check whether caching is working?
options: The HTTP status code
cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens in the response usage
The model name in the response
The max_tokens setting
quiz.explanation: The usage object reports tokens written to and read from the cache on every response.

quiz.question: A research assistant’s hit rate is 40%. Which changes could raise it? Select all that apply.
options: Move the analyst’s name and the date after the breakpoint
Keep tool definitions in a fixed order
Group questions about the same report close together in time
Put the question before the report
quiz.explanation: Stable, identically ordered prefixes and calls within the lifetime raise hits. Putting the question first breaks the prefix.

quiz.question: Base input is $3 per million tokens. A call reads a 10,000-token prefix from cache at 0.1× and adds 500 new input tokens. What is the input cost of the call?
What is the key difference between prompt caching and semantic response caching?
options: Semantic caching regenerates the answer each time
Both skip the model entirely
Prompt caching reuses the processed prefix but the model still generates a fresh answer
Neither uses stored data
quiz.explanation: Prompt caching only discounts repeated input. A semantic cache returns a stored answer without calling the model.
